message.content:
Below is a quick‑start “recipe” that shows **two** common ways to grab a PNG of whatever is rendered in Google Chrome: | Goal | What you’ll need | Quick code | |------|------------------|------------| | **Take a screenshot of a *new* page** (you control the URL) | `selenium` + a Chrome driver (`webdriver‑manager` makes it painless) | ```python
from selenium import webdriver
from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager

# 1️⃣ Start Chrome (headless optional)
options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument("--headless") # comment out if you want a visible window
driver = webdriver.Chrome(ChromeDriverManager().install(), options=options)

# 2️⃣ Go to the page you want to capture
driver.get("https://www.example.com")

# 3️⃣ Grab the screenshot – Selenium does the heavy lifting for you
driver.save_screenshot("page.png")
# 4️⃣ Clean up
driver.quit()
``` | | **Grab whatever is already showing in an *existing* Chrome window** | Launch Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` (or any free port). Then use the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) – e.g. via `pychrome` or a raw `requests` call. | ```python
import base64, json, time, requests
import pychrome # pip install pychrome

# 1️⃣ Make sure Chrome is running with remote debugging enabled:
# chrome.exe --remote-debugging-port=9222\n# (On macOS/Linux: /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222)\n\n# 2️⃣ Connect to the CDP endpoint\nbrowser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222")\n\n# 3️⃣ Pick the tab you want – here we just grab the first one\n# You can filter by tab.title or tab.url if you know what you’re looking for\nfor t in browser.list_tab():\n print(t.id, t.title, t.url)\n\n# 4️⃣ Attach to the tab and capture a screenshot\nif browser.list_tab():\n tab = browser.list_tab()[0] # or pick by title/url\n tab.start() # start the tab’s event loop\n # Optional: navigate to a URL if you want to refresh the page\n # tab.call_method(\"Page.navigate\", url=\"https://www.example.com\")\n # tab.wait(5) # wait for the page to load\n\n # Capture the screenshot – the result is a base64‑encoded PNG\n result = tab.call_method(\"Page.captureScreenshot\", format=\"png\", quality=100)\n img_data = base64.b64decode(result[\"data\"])\n with open(\"current_page.png\", \"wb\") as f:\n f.write(img_data)\n tab.stop()\nelse:\n print(\"No tabs found – did you start Chrome with --remote-debugging-port?\")\n``` | --- ### Why use CDP instead of Selenium? * **Selenium can’t attach to an already‑running Chrome instance** – it always starts a fresh browser (unless you use a special “attach” feature that requires a pre‑configured debugging port). * CDP gives you *direct* access to Chrome’s internal APIs, so you can capture the exact rendering that Chrome is showing, even if you didn’t navigate there yourself. --- ## Step‑by‑step walk‑through 1. **Install the helper libraries** ```bash pip install selenium webdriver-manager pychrome ``` 2. **Launch Chrome with remote debugging** *Windows* ```cmd "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` *macOS* ```bash /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` *Linux* ```bash google-chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` Leave this window open while your script runs. 3. **Run the script** *If you’re using the Selenium route*, just run the snippet above – it will open a *new* Chrome window (headless if you added that flag) and save a screenshot. *If you’re using the CDP route*, make sure the script points at the correct debugging URL (`http://127.0.0.1:9222`). It will list all open tabs, pick the first one, and write a PNG of whatever is currently rendered. --- ## Common pitfalls & troubleshooting | Symptom | Fix | |---------|-----| | `pychrome.exceptions.PyChromeException: No tab found` | Did you actually start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port`? Check that the port is open (`netstat -an | grep 9222` on Linux/macOS). | | Screenshot is blank or only a few pixels | The page may not have finished loading. Add a short `time.sleep(5)` after navigation or use `tab.wait(5)` to give it time. | | You see a “blocked by policy” error when trying to capture a screenshot of a site that uses CSP or mixed‑content restrictions | CDP bypasses most CSP checks, but if the page is protected by a login you’ll need to log in first (e.g. via Selenium or by sending the appropriate cookies). | | You want a *specific* area of the page (e.g. a div) | Pass a `clip` argument to `Page.captureScreenshot`: `clip={"x":0,"y":0,"width":800,"height":600}`. See the [Chrome DevTools Protocol docs](https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/tot/Page/#method-captureScreenshot). | --- ## Bonus: Grab a screenshot of *just the visible viewport* (no scrolling) Both Selenium and CDP capture the full page by default. To capture only what’s visible on the screen: * **Selenium** – add `fullPage=False` (in newer Selenium versions) or simply use the default (it captures the viewport). ```python driver.save_screenshot("viewport.png") # captures the viewport ``` * **CDP** – set `captureBeyondViewport` to `False` (default) and optionally pass a `clip` rectangle. ```python result = tab.call_method( "Page.captureScreenshot", format="png", quality=100, clip={"x":0,"y":0,"width":800,"height":600} ) ``` --- ## TL;DR * **New page → Selenium** – simplest, works out of the box. * **Existing tab → CDP (`pychrome`)** – attach to a running Chrome instance and call `Page.captureScreenshot`. * **Screen capture (any app)** – `pyautogui.screenshot()` if you just need a quick “take a picture of the screen” solution. Pick the approach that matches whether you control the URL or you need to capture whatever the user is already looking at. Happy screenshotting!
